clue.text: Drained of colour, suddenly

definitions.meaning: read literally: with the blue taken out
the everyday idiom for without warning

explanation.surface: Something goes pale all at once, like a face losing its colour in shock.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical literal reading of the phrase: whatever has had the blue drained away is out of the blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of the blue means unexpectedly, which is what suddenly means.

clue.text: Test going round part — of the M25?

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: An exam going round part of London's great ring road, as if the test were a traffic survey.
explanation.walkthrough: The M25 is the motorway ringing London, known as the London Orbital; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The M25 circles London, so something of the M25 is orbital, running in a ring.

clue.text: Evidently sore after hit on the bottom, one whacked

indicators.note: after places the sore colour behind the other letters
in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the word whose last letter is taken
I is the Roman numeral for one
a sore spot looks red, so red is what sore evidently is

explanation.surface: Someone smacked on the backside is visibly sore, a beaten figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the bottom' takes the last letter of 'hit', T; I (one) follows, and 'after' puts RED (evidently sore) at the end. 'Whacked' is British slang for exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Whacked is informal British slang for exhausted, worn out, so it means tired.

clue.text: Money about right, weapon for charger without contract

parts.note: a knight's weapon when charging on horseback

explanation.surface: A mercenary knight weighs up his pay and his lance while riding without any contract.
explanation.walkthrough: The word freelance began as a mercenary knight, a lance free to hire, so the surface's charger is historically apt.
explanation.definitionFit: A freelance works for many clients without a permanent employment contract.

clue.text: Cover carpet, surface unseen

indicators.note: the top or surface letter of the word, in a down entry its first, cannot be seen, so it is removed

parts.note: to carpet someone is to reprimand them, to chide

explanation.surface: Covering a carpet so that its surface cannot be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carpet' is a verb here: to scold. 'surface unseen' removes its top letter, C.
explanation.definitionFit: A hide is a covered shelter for watching birds, or an animal's skin; to hide is to cover or conceal.

clue.text: Singer, Scot for example, entertaining American individual

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to hold them within

parts.note: a Scot is one kind of Brit

explanation.surface: A Scottish singer hosts a visiting American.
explanation.walkthrough: Singer in the surface names a performer, and it is simply the definition; the Scot is only there to be a Brit.
explanation.definitionFit: A baritone is a male singer with a voice between tenor and bass.

clue.text: Your bank's shut in town

definitions.note: town is used as a modifier (town planning), matching the adjective urban

indicators.note: the answer is enclosed within the words before it

explanation.surface: Your bank branch has closed its doors in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Shut in reads like a closed-down branch; here it tells you the answer is shut inside the other words.
explanation.definitionFit: Town used as a modifier, as in town life or town planning, carries the same sense as the Latin-derived adjective for built-up places.

clue.text: Englishman abroad with queen, one's scented

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a noun: one (a thing) that is scented

parts.note: Australian slang for an English person

explanation.surface: An English traveller and a queen, one of whom wears perfume.
explanation.walkthrough: Abroad points to how Australians and New Zealanders call the English Poms.
explanation.definitionFit: A pomander is a ball of perfumed substances, a thing that is scented.

clue.text: Loom I fix that conserves power

explanation.surface: A weaver repairs a loom in an energy-saving way.
explanation.walkthrough: Loom sits first as a noun for a weaving frame, but it is the verb, to hang over threateningly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that impends looms, threatening to happen soon.

clue.text: Halt in trade for landlord, say

parts.note: legal tender is what is accepted in trade

explanation.surface: A publican is ordered to stop dealing.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a landlord is also the keeper of a pub, and the say marks him as an example of someone serving drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub landlord pours the drinks, so he is one example of a bartender.

clue.text: Report about opening of leaf in flower

indicators.note: about means the report goes around the leaf's first letter

parts.note: a boom is a loud report, a bang

indicators.note: opening means the first letter

parts.note: the word whose opening is taken

explanation.surface: A description of a leaf unfurling in a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: BOOM (a report, as of a gun) goes 'about' L, the 'opening of' leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloom is a flower, especially one on a cultivated plant.

clue.text: Little worse for wear

explanation.surface: Someone is a bit the worse for wear.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together, the clue says slightly drunk, which is itself the second sense; tiddly is British slang both for tiny and for a bit tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiddly means very small, and also mildly drunk.

clue.text: Neanderthal figure breaks leg

parts.note: a leg of a journey is a stage

explanation.surface: A caveman figure snaps his leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Figure looks like a body, but it is a number.
explanation.definitionFit: Neanderthal, used as an adjective for something primitive, means stone-age.

clue.text: Regret seeing people from Los Angeles ending in Pontefract

indicators.note: the end letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Californians rue their journey finishing in a Yorkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Pontefract is a small town in Yorkshire, England, a comic comedown from Los Angeles.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to express sorrow over something past is both to regret and to lament it.

clue.text: Bone thrown in heap on the way out

indicators.note: something thrown in lands inside the heap, so the bone ends up enclosed by it

explanation.surface: A bone tossed on the pile as it leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Bone and heap together suggest a graveyard, which suits a word meaning dying.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: on the way out describes anything close to death or obsolescence, which is the Latin-rooted word's sense of dying.

clue.text: Fixed indeed, so probably a foregone conclusion?

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase describing a contest; the answer is the adjective for such a contest

indicators.note: fixing rearranges things, as a rigged result is fixed

explanation.surface: A match that was rigged is naturally a foregone conclusion.
explanation.walkthrough: The so looks like part of the fodder's sentence, and it is: both indeed and so are rearranged. A one-sided contest has an outcome known in advance.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-sided contest is so unequal that its result is all but certain.

clue.text: Bad taste, pig stuffed with hot Italian food

indicators.note: stuffed with means the jumbled letters have a further letter packed inside them
bad signals that the letters of taste and pig are spoiled, jumbled into a new order

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A gourmet's verdict: poor taste, a pig stuffed and served with something spicy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad taste' reads as a verdict, but 'Bad' is the signal to rearrange; the H for hot goes into the jumble just after its G, giving SPAGETTI 'stuffed with' H.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is long thin pasta, a staple of Italian cooking.

clue.text: Piper cares to play organ

parts.note: Pan, the Greek god, plays the pan pipes

indicators.note: to play means the letters of cares are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: A piper is keen to play the organ.
explanation.walkthrough: PAN is the piping god; 'to play' rearranges CARES to CREAS. 'Organ' looks musical here, but it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The pancreas is a gland organ behind the stomach that produces insulin and digestive enzymes.

clue.text: Rider Haggard's first novel a sermon

indicators.note: first means take the first letter

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of a sermon are freshly arranged

explanation.surface: Novelist Rider Haggard's debut book is a sermon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rider' looks like part of the name H. Rider Haggard, but it is the definition. H is Haggard's 'first', then 'novel' rearranges A SERMON to ORSEMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A horseman is a rider of horses.

clue.text: Plague in shelter regularly, donkey quarantined

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so only letters spaced evenly through the word are kept

explanation.surface: An animal is kept isolated in a shelter during a plague outbreak.
explanation.walkthrough: Plague looks like the disease that makes quarantine necessary, but it is the verb, to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: to keep bothering someone is to plague them, the informal word being the modern equivalent.

clue.text: Blight on rank vegetable

indicators.note: one piece is placed on the next in the across entry

explanation.surface: Disease strikes a foul-smelling vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: Blight and rank both suggest rot in the garden; they are the verb to spoil and a line of things. A marrow is a large squash grown in British gardens.
explanation.definitionFit: A marrow is a large vegetable of the squash family.

clue.text: Thingummy that now needs repairing

indicators.note: the letters must be put together again

explanation.surface: Some gadget whose name escapes you is now broken.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the everyday frustration of a broken thing you cannot name, and the answer is one of the words for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A whatnot, like a thingummy, is a word for something whose name you cannot recall.

clue.text: Take time with two vehicles reversing

indicators.note: the whole string runs backwards

explanation.surface: Take your time while two cars are backing up.
explanation.walkthrough: Take is the arithmetic sense, as in take four from ten.
explanation.definitionFit: The arithmetic sense: in take four from ten, take means to remove one number from another.

clue.text: Roof blown off farmhouse, sweep

indicators.note: in a down entry the roof is the top letter, so the first letter goes

parts.note: a grange is a country house with farm buildings, a farmhouse

explanation.surface: A gale tears the roof off a farmhouse, sweeping across the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roof blown off' removes the top letter, G, from GRANGE (farmhouse).
explanation.definitionFit: A range is a sweep or extent, as in a wide sweep of view or a range of hills.

clue.text: Dread playing hit, ostensibly Brothers in Arms, first of all

indicators.note: the first letter of each word

parts.words: playing hit, ostensibly Brothers in Arms
parts.note: Playing Hit Ostensibly Brothers In Arms

explanation.surface: Someone dreads hearing Dire Straits' big hit played again.
explanation.walkthrough: Brothers in Arms is a 1985 Dire Straits album and song, which is why ostensibly and hit are there.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an irrational, overwhelming fear of something, such as spiders or heights, is a dread.

clue.text: Brightness initially with shortage in dark

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the word's first letter is used

explanation.surface: A shortage of light leaves things dark.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is almost a description of the answer: brightness in short supply leaves black.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a night with no light at all is dark, or at its extreme, pitch black.

clue.text: Embroidered, fake news

indicators.note: a fake is a false version, the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A story has been embellished, making it fake news.
explanation.walkthrough: Embroidered in the surface means exaggerated, as in an embroidered tale; the answer takes it literally, as needlework.
explanation.definitionFit: The literal needlework sense: decoration stitched onto cloth with thread has been embroidered, i.e. worked with a needle.

clue.text: Stripe on new pillowcases etc

explanation.surface: A stripe printed on new pillowcases.
explanation.walkthrough: Linen here is household bedding in general, not only the fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Pillowcases, sheets and the like are bed linen.

clue.text: Try and see in when blurry, nursing a pain from looking?

indicators.note: nursing means holding, so the jumbled letters cradle the a inside
and gathers try with see in, so all three words go into the same blurred pool of letters
blurry vision confuses the letters, so try, see and in are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to someone with blurred vision: try to see in, though looking hurts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' gathers TRY with SEE IN, and 'when blurry' rearranges them to EYESTRIN, which is 'nursing' A.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyestrain is fatigue or ache of the eyes caused by prolonged looking or reading.

clue.text: Ice skates not designed for series of passes

indicators.note: the letters are designed into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Skates unsuited to a run of passing moves, as in ice hockey.
explanation.walkthrough: NOT is part of the fodder and designed alone is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A season ticket covers a whole series of admissions or journeys.
